025.subtitle: Elephants that attend her, cavalry that encircles her

commentary.meaning: Two names again, sixteen syllables each, one to a line, and this time constructed as matched panels. The preceding verse announced in general terms that she moves with an army of her own powers; this verse begins the roll-call, and it begins with the two divisions that a classical Indian army was measured by. Sampatkarī, whose name means the maker of prosperity, rides at the head of the elephants. Aśvārūḍhā, whose name means no more than the one mounted on a horse, commands a cavalry counted in a figure nobody is expected to add up. Both names use the same participle for being mounted, which makes the parallel unmistakable, and then they diverge in their final words, exactly and meaningfully: the elephants attend her, the horses enclose her. One is a retinue and the other a perimeter. Two of the four traditional divisions of an army are named here and the remaining two are held back, so that the order of battle assembles gradually rather than arriving in a single list.
commentary.history:
Sampatkarī and Aśvārūḍhā are named goddesses in the Lalitopākhyāna, not personifications invented for the verse, and both have an independent life in Śrīvidyā practice, with their own mantras and their own place in the ritual invocation of Lalitā's retinue. Their function in the narrative is military and specific: one commands the elephant division, the other the cavalry. The retellings give names to their mounts as well, though such details vary between versions and are the first thing to shift in transmission. What does not vary is the structure — the goddess does not fight alone, and the powers that fight for her are individuated, named, and given commands.

The classical Indian army had four arms, and the word for it, caturaṅga, means simply four-limbed: elephants, chariots, cavalry, and foot. The word travelled westward with the game modelled on that army and became, by a long chain of borrowings, the English word chess. Naming the elephants first is conventional and reflects their actual standing, since an elephant corps was the most expensive and the most prestigious component of a kingdom's force, the thing a ruler was assessed by. That standing is why the goddess who leads them is called the maker of prosperity. The association between elephants and wealth is not decorative in Indian thought: Śrī herself is shown flanked by elephants pouring water over her, and the elephant is the standing emblem of royal abundance. Sampad, the word inside her name, covers prosperity, attainment and abundance in the broad sense, and pairing it with the elephant division makes the point that the wealth of a kingdom and the force of a kingdom were, in practice, the same asset.

The vocabulary of the first name repays attention. Sindhura is one of the many Sanskrit words for elephant, and vraja is a herd or pen — the same word that gives Vraja, the cowherd country of Kṛṣṇa's childhood, a place named after its cattle enclosures. Sevitā, waited upon, is from the root sev, to attend or serve, which also gives sevā, the ordinary word for service in a temple or to a teacher. So the elephants are not merely present; they are described in the vocabulary of liturgical attendance.

The second name is built out of the same materials and does something different with them. Adhiṣṭhita, presided over, is formed from the root sthā with the prefix adhi, over — the same root that supplied the words for abiding and standing in the verses about her dwelling, now shifted from location to command. Koṭi is a real number, ten million, the largest of the older Indian numerals in common use, and doubling it into koṭikoṭi is an idiom for a quantity past counting rather than a vague gesture at largeness; the tradition prefers hyperbole that has been arithmetically specified. And āvṛtā, surrounded, comes from the root vṛ with the prefix ā, to cover or enclose — which is precisely the root behind āvaraṇa, the technical term for the nine enclosures of the Śrīcakra. The word chosen to say that cavalry rings her is the word used for the concentric rings of the diagram. Whether the hymn intends the echo or simply reaches for the natural word, the effect for a practitioner is the same: the army in formation and the yantra on the altar have the same shape, a centre with rings around it, and the enclosing is done in both cases by her own powers.

One textual matter. The nāmāvalī transmitted with this text writes the elephant word as sindura rather than sindhura, dropping the aspiration. Sindūra is a genuine Sanskrit word — it means vermilion, the red lead used as a cosmetic and in worship — but it is not what the compound requires, and the reading is most likely a slip of transmission rather than a variant with meaning behind it. It is the sort of thing worth knowing about before comparing two printed texts and concluding that one of them is wrong about something important.
commentary.practice:
These two names are the best-matched pair in this part of the hymn, and the efficient way to learn them is together. Both open with a goddess's name, continue with a participle meaning mounted, then give the animal and the multitude, and close with a participle describing what that multitude does. Hold that frame in mind and the sixteen syllables stop being a wall.

The joints of the first name are sampatkarī, samārūḍha, sindhura, vraja, sevitā; of the second, aśvārūḍhā, adhiṣṭhita, aśva, koṭikoṭibhiḥ, āvṛtā. The second involves three sandhis, all worth seeing rather than memorising. Long ā plus short a gives long ā, so the join in aśvārūḍhādhiṣṭhita is silent; two short a's likewise give one long ā, giving adhiṣṭhitāśva; and a visarga after i, before a voiced sound, becomes r, hence koṭikoṭibhir āvṛtā.

That last point carries a grammatical fact: this name is not one word. The compound ends at koṭikoṭi, in the instrumental plural, and āvṛtā is a separate participle governing it. Knowing where the boundary falls makes the name easier to hold.

The consonants are the hardest in this stretch of the stotra. Ḍh, the voiced aspirated retroflex, appears in both names: tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth, voiced, with breath released after it. Ṣṭh in adhiṣṭhita is retroflex sibilant into aspirated retroflex stop, both with the tongue back, and is the most difficult conjunct here. Śv appears twice, palatal sibilant into v. Ndh in sindhura is dental n into aspirated dh. Vr in vraja is v into a full r, and vṛ in āvṛtā is v into the vocalic ṛ, itself a syllable.

Sampatkarī conceals a discrepancy between how Devanāgarī writes the name and how it is said. The script groups it as sa, mpa, tka, rī, but the syllables are sam, pat, ka, rī: the m closes the first syllable and the t the second. Written conjuncts often straddle a syllable boundary in this way, and a learner who treats the written units as spoken ones will produce something unrecognisable.

Koṭikoṭi is worth noticing as sound and not only as arithmetic. The o is long and the i of ṭi is short, so the four syllables come out long, short, long, short over a repeated retroflex ṭ. In a name about cavalry it falls into a gallop, and there is no reason to resist that.

For archanā both names take the ordinary dative: sampatkarīsamārūḍhasindhuravrajasevitāyai namaḥ, aśvārūḍhādhiṣṭhitāśvakoṭikoṭibhirāvṛtāyai namaḥ. If a printed nāmāvalī gives sindura, that is the transmission slip described above rather than a choice to be made.

What the verse asks is symmetry. Two names of identical length and near-identical construction, delivered at the same weight, produce the effect the poet built — two divisions parading past in matched order, and rushing the second because the first was hard destroys it. There is one thing to hold while chanting that second name: the word saying the horses surround her is the word used for the rings of the diagram, so the name tells you what those enclosures are made of.

crossReferences.deva: अश्वपूर्वां रथमध्यां हस्तिनादप्रबोधिनीम् । श्रियं देवीमुपह्वये श्रीर्मा देवी जुषताम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: aśvapūrvāṃ rathamadhyāṃ hastinādaprabodhinīm | śriyaṃ devīm upahvaye śrīr mā devī juṣatām ||
crossReferences.translation: Her whose van is horses, whose centre is chariots, who is wakened by the trumpeting of elephants — the goddess Śrī I call here; may the goddess Śrī take pleasure in me.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest form of the association this verse is working with, and it puts the same three arms in the same order. Śrī is prosperity itself, and she is described in the vocabulary of a marching column: horses in front, chariots in the middle, elephants loud enough to wake her. That a hymn asking for wealth should describe wealth as an army in motion explains why the goddess who leads the elephants in the Lalitā narrative is named the maker of prosperity, and why the two ideas need no bridge between them.

crossReferences.deva: सर्वस्वरूपे सर्वेशे सर्वशक्तिसमन्विते । भयेभ्यस्त्राहि नो देवि दुर्गे देवि नमोऽस्तु ते ॥
crossReferences.iast: sarvasvarūpe sarveśe sarvaśaktisamanvite | bhayebhyas trāhi no devi durge devi namo'stu te ||
crossReferences.translation: You whose form is everything, ruler of everything, attended by every power — save us from what we fear, goddess. Durgā, goddess, homage to you.
crossReferences.relevance: Sarvaśaktisamanvite, attended by every power, is the same construction the sahasranāma used one verse earlier for her army of śaktis, and it shows what the roll-call of divisions is for. The petition is not that she should have troops but that the person praying should be on the inside of them. Placed beside the elephants and the cavalry, it identifies what the enumeration is doing emotionally as well as narratively: a reciter surrounded by a description of a perimeter is being shown where safety is.

references.title: Śrī Sūkta
references.author: transmitted as a khila, a supplementary hymn appended to the Ṛgveda rather than part of the Saṃhitā proper; printed with translation in most South Indian ritual manuals
references.note: Fifteen or so verses, chanted constantly in temple and household worship, and the earliest sustained address to the goddess of prosperity in Sanskrit. Worth reading through in one sitting for the concreteness of what it asks for — cattle, gold, servants, food — which is a corrective to the assumption that a name like Sampatkarī must be an allegory for something more refined.

references.title: Elephants and Kings: An Environmental History
references.author: Thomas R. Trautmann (University of Chicago Press, 2015)
references.note: An unexpected but genuinely useful book here. Trautmann explains why Indian kingdoms went to enormous expense to maintain elephant corps, how elephants were captured and kept, and why the elephant became the emblem of royal wealth rather than merely a weapon. After reading it, the pairing of an elephant division with a goddess named for prosperity looks like a statement about political economy rather than a poetic flourish.

references.title: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (Ancient Indian Tradition and Mythology series)
references.author: tr. G. V. Tagare (Motilal Banarsidass, 1983–84)
references.note: The Lalitopākhyāna gives the order of battle at length, with the divisions, their commanders and their mounts. Reading it alongside these verses shows how much the hymn is compressing, and also how much it is selecting: several figures who occupy long passages of the narrative get no name in the stotra at all.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Sir Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Four entries make this verse legible: sindhura, one of a startling number of Sanskrit words for elephant; vraja, which is a herd before it is a place name; koṭi, to see that it is a definite numeral and not a synonym for many; and the root vṛ with the prefix ā, which is where the connection between being surrounded and the enclosures of the Śrīcakra becomes visible.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with the Saubhāgyabhāskara of Bhāskararāya
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library / Theosophical Publishing House)
references.note: Indispensable through the war names, where a modern reader has the least chance of recognising who is being referred to. The commentary identifies the attendant goddesses and connects them to their places in the ritual invocation, which is the information that turns a list of troops into a description of something a practitioner does.
